PASSENGER TRAFFIC",,"Is the effort, being made by the Canadian National Railways, to regain passenger traffic proving at all successful and (a) if not, does the railway plan to continue the effort (b) if so, why is passenger train service, such as trains 3 and 4 between Saskatoon and Vancouver, being discontinued?
Answer by: Mr. McBain:
The management of Canadian National Railways advise as follows:

It is the objective of the company to compete vigorously for passenger business in those areas where facilities and size of the travel market provide a reasonable expectation that the company can realize a profit by so doing, and to withdraw from those services that in spite of reasonable efforts do not produce sufficient revenues to offset their operating costs and have no reasonable prospect of doing so.

With reference to part (b) of the question certain adjustments are being made in train services all across the system in keeping with the travel demand throughout the winter season. These changes become effective with the fall timetable change October 28, 1962 (this is normal practice throughout the railway industry generally).

column2: Does the Department of Citizenship and Immigration refuse or delay applications made by Canadian citizens of Chinese origin to bring their fiancees, wives, or other relatives to Canada as sponsored immigrants in cases where the department is not satisfied as to the true identity of such Canadian citizens or as to the legality of their original entry into Canada?
Does the department refuse or delay applications made by persons of Chinese origin eligible for entry to Canada under section 31(a) of the

column1: immigration regulations in cases where such persons are related to Canadian citizens or residents of Canada of whose identity or of the legality of whose entry to Canada the department has some doubt?
Answer by: Mr. McGee:

column2: In all cases involving an application to bring a sponsored immigrant to Canada the bona tides of the applicant, his true identity, and the true identity and relationship to the applicant of the prospective immigrant must be satisfactorily established before a determination can be made of the admissibility of the proposed immigrant under the regulations. If the identity of the sponsor is in doubt, it follows that his true relationship to the proposed immigrant cannot be established until those doubts are removed. Instances have arisen in which it has been established that the applicant has entered Canada and later obtained a Canadian citizenship certificate under a false identity. It is not possible for such applicants to sponsor the admission of others without first clearing up their own identity.

Immigrants admitted under section 31(a) of the immigration regulations may be sponsored or unsponsored. With respect to those sponsored under the provisions of section 31(a) (iv) the answer is as in (1) above.

column1: The existence of relatives in Canada whose identity may be in doubt would not prejudice the application of an unsponsored immigrant applying under section 31(a) (i), (ii) or (iii), who could satisfactorily establish his own identity and meet the other requirements of the Immigration Act and regulations.

2182335,ca.proc.d.1962-10-24.1.13.1,1962-10-24,31f9003f-61b2-46f3-8583-3537e0560943,ca.m.5988,,,QUESTIONS,SKIING IN ATLANTIC PROVINCES NATIONAL PARKS,,1. What steps has the government taken to add skiing to the present facilities of any of the national parks in the Atlantic provinces?

column2: Has any report been received on the feasibility of ski runs in the Atlantic provinces national parks?
Has the government received any representation since January 1, 1962, from any person or groups relating to this matter and, if so, when, from whom, and to what general effect?

column1: Answer by: Mr. Dinsdale:

1 and 2. In the fall of 1961, arrangements were made for a ski expert, Mr. Franz Baier, to undertake a technical survey of the hills in Fundy and Cape Breton Highlands national parks to determine their potential for ski purposes.

Reports have been received from Mr. Baier on the feasibility of ski developments in these two national parks. His technical assessment covered four sites in Cape Breton Highlands national park as well as a number of sites outside the boundaries of the park in the bay St. Lawrence area. The sites within the park are located at Clyburn brook, McIntosh brook, north Aspy and south Mountain. Only the north Aspy and south Mountain sites were considered to be technically suited. In the light of such other factors as long range development planning, economic feasibility and park concepts, it was decided that South Mountain was the only site that could be considered for development.

The technical report on Fundy national park indicated that there were no sites in the park that could be developed into good public and recreational skiing areas. There were no hills or slopes with northern exposure that had the required length, degree of slope or smooth average ground surface. Nevertheless, the report mentioned the possibility that a week end skiing site might be developed at Alcorn hill but indicated that snow conditions are normally quite unreliable. The report also stated that two areas outside the park-Albert and the Elgin and South branch -had far greater potential for development.

column2: During January and February of this year I received representations from several members of this house, including the hon.

column1: member for Saint John-Albert, the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria and the former member for Westmorland. During the same period, representations were received as well from Mr. W. A. N. Macdonald, tourist co-ordinator for the southeastern New Brunswick tourist bureau and from Mr. Douglas Mahon of Halifax. I also held discussions with interested individuals in the areas concerned and with representatives from local chambers of commerce. In all of these representations, information was sought as to the feasibility of developing skiing facilities in Cape Breton Highlands and Fundy national parks.

PAYMENT FOR WINTER WORKS",,"Have all the municipalities of the county of Chapleau, which have had works done under the winter works program during the 1961-62 season been reimbursed, and, if not, why; and when will they be reimbursed?
Answer by: Mr. Hales:

Under the municipal winter works incentive program for 1961-1962, 24 projects submitted by municipalities in the county of Chapleau were accepted. Final statements of claim have been submitted by the province in respect to 19 of these projects. Payment of 15 of these claims has been made to the province and payment of the other four will be made within the course of the next day or so.
In addition, interim claims have been submitted by the province in respect to three of the other projects. Payment of two of these
interim claims has been made to the province and payment of the other one will be going forward within a day or so.
No claims have as yet been received in respect to two of the projects authorized.
All federal payments under the municipal winter works incentive program are made to the province for reimbursement to the municipalities.

,Social Credit,,Mr. Laprise,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=9b3dd9d2-7778-4d49-a34d-5f5d73259bfd&Language=E&Section=ALL
2182363,ca.proc.d.1962-10-24.1.24.2,1962-10-24,44e56019-054f-454f-bffd-55c0f1f3819a,ca.m.8378,Mr. Halpenny:,Secretary of State of Canada,QUESTIONS,* BILINGUAL REQUIREMENT, CIVIL SERVICE VACANCIES",,"In establishing language qualifications required of persons appointed to the civil service, the civil service commission is governed by the provisions of Section 47 of the Civil Service Act which states in part ""that the number of employees .. .who are qualified in the knowledge and use of the English of French language or both, shall.. .be sufficient to enable the department or local office to perform its functions adequately and to give effective service to the public"".

In carrying out this statutory injunction the commission, as a matter of practice, normally requires that all employees be bilingual in an office where the minority, English or French speaking, of the persons served by that office exceeds 40 per cent of the total population served by that office. Where the minority served by an office is less than 40 per cent of the total population served, then the commission normally requires that employees knowledgeable in the use of both languages be at approximately the same proportion to the whole office staff as the minority is to the total number of persons served.

column2: Since July 4, 1961, when the Prime Minister spoke of the critical character of the Berlin crisis, how many military personnel have been returned to Canada from Europe?
How many wives and children of Canadian servicemen are now residing in Germany?
What provisions have been made for the safety of these dependents in the event of the outbreak of war in Germany?
Does the Berlin situation warrant a re-examination of the cut-back program in service strength?

column1: Answer by Mr. Harkness:

column2: Provision for the safety of dependants in Europe cannot be guaranteed. However, there are plans for their dispersal to selected areas or evacuation from the continent. The carrying out of these plans would depend on the type of emergency which might arise.
Plans are being reviewed to meet all possible contingencies.

SET-OFF YARD, TORONTO",,"Have representations been received from the Aldershot property owners association in opposition to the site selected for a proposed set-off yard of the Canadian National Railways and (a) if so, has the company taken any action in an effort to find an alternative site (b) if not, will the
Questions
minister request that the company give immediate consideration to the desirability of finding an alternative site?
Answer by: Mr. McBain:
The management of Canadian National Railways advise as follows:

Representations have been received and officers of the great lakes region have held meetings with the mayor and councillors in order to explain what is involved. The existing main line through Burlington was constructed in 1855, and the planned set-off tracks are an essential part of the operations to serve the industrial complex between Burlington and Mimico and the connection with the line to the new hump yard. The railway officers have made an extensive examination of the situation as to the location of the set-off tracks and several sites were examined in the course of which many factors had to be taken into account such as operating conditions, and engineering limitations. Every effort has been made in the over-all project in order that the minimum of disturbance would be caused to communities.

column2: Since the coming into force of the Unemployment Insurance Act, did any firms adopt the ""rotation time off schedule"" (e.g., five weeks work, one week off) instead of fully laying off a specified number of men, and, if so, did the unemployment insurance commission on such occasion grant any concession covering the one week waiting period for benefits?
At what date, and by what firms, was the ""rotation time off schedule"" adopted; and at what times, and for the employees of which firm, did the commission grant concessions under (1) above?

column1: Answer by: Mr. Hales:

column2: Several firms have followed a work pattern whereby their employees worked one or more full weeks followed by a lay-off of a week or more and, after serving the waiting period, these employees were paid unemployment insurance benefit in respect of the week(s) of unemployment.

column1: No concessions have been made by the commission with respect to the waiting period in such circumstances.

It is pointed out, however, that section 152 of the unemployment insurance regulations provides for waiving of the waiting period under certain conditions when a new claim immediately follows the termination of a previous claim, and this has been used where applicable.

column2: No record is kept of the firms who have followed a rotation pattern of work, and, as already stated, no concessions have been granted respecting the waiting period.

United States citizens temporarily resident in Canada on summer property, whether or not they commute to employment in the United States, are admitted as non-immigrant visitors.

column2: The period of non-immigrant entry for persons mentioned in this question normally expires on or before October 31 of each year, which is regarded as the end of the summer season. Persons in this category who satisfy the immigration officers concerned that they are in fact bona fide temporary residents, as distinct from permanent residents, may be allowed entry beyond October 31. If it is established that any persons originally admitted as temporary visitors have in fact become permanent residents, they are examined as immigrants. This is not a new policy or practice of the department.
Citizens of the United States do not require visas for entry to Canada. As indicated in the answer to question 2, temporary entry may be granted beyond October 31 to bona fide non-immigrants.

I direct a question to the Minister of National Revenue. In asking this question I have considered those matters to which the Prime Minister adverted a few moments ago.

Can the minister tell the house whether a Cubana Airlines aircraft with two East German technicians aboard landed at Goose Bay, Labrador, this morning, and was searched by customs officials assisted by the R.C.M.P.? If so, was this done in order to facilitate the United States quarantine of Cuba?

,New Democratic Party,,Thomas Rodney Berger,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b4ec6d8f-edc9-4275-b515-1f3f5c59870d&Language=E&Section=ALL

Green (Secretary of Stale for External Affairs):,Secretary of State for External Affairs,EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,GOOSE BAY, LABRADOR  SEARCH OF CUBAN PLANE",,"Perhaps a word of explanation on this question would be helpful. For some time now the government has been concerned at the increasing number of Soviet aircraft requesting landing or overflight privileges in Canada en route to Cuba. This privilege is one which is normally accorded on a reciprocal basis under the ICAO convention and related agreements to which the Soviet union is not a signatory.

We have informed the Soviet union that since this right is a privilege stemming from an agreement to which they are not a party, no further landings in Canada or overflights of Canadian territory will be granted to Soviet aircraft en route to Cuba.

With respect to flights between other Soviet bloc countries and Cuba, we have taken steps to ensure that inspection and other relevant procedures in accordance with Canadian laws and the provisions of the ICAO convention are fully complied with to ensure that no warlike material is being carried through Canada to Cuba. Under the ICAO convention, no munitions of war or implements of war may be carried in or above the territory of a state in aircraft engaged in international navigation, except by permission of such state. Canadian law contains a similar provision.

With respect to the reports which have appeared this morning, I can confirm that an aircraft owned by Cubana Airlines landed last night at Goose Bay airport on its way from Prague to Havana. It was searched by
Inquiries of the Ministry the Canadian customs authorities and nothing of an objectionable nature was found in its cargo. The aircraft has now been allowed to proceed to Havana.

At the present time, neither the United States quarantine of Cuba nor Canadian policy in this regard contain any restrictions on the normal movement of personnel into Cuba. For the time being we are concerned only with weapons, and this, I believe, is also the position of the United States.

,Progressive Conservative,,Howard Charles Green,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=6dec82d6-fab3-438b-b40f-c7720a93d8c1&Language=E&Section=ALL

2182648,ca.proc.d.1962-10-24.36.1.1,1962-10-24,,,,stagedirection,,,,Resolved,-that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Income Tax Act to provide among other things:

column2: That for the 1962 and subsequent taxation years the amount deductible in computing taxable income in respect of a child qualified for family allowance be increased to $300 and the amount deductible in respect of other dependants be increased to $550 each.

That with respect to income earned after March 31, 1962 a corporation whose principal business is manufacturing or processing (not including a corporation whose principal business is shipbuilding, mining, logging or the operation of oil or gas wells) be allowed to deduct from its tax otherwise payable an amount equal to 50 per cent of the tax on the first $50,000, of its taxable income attributable to increased sales and an amount equal to 25 per cent of the tax on the remainder of its taxable income so attributable.

That with respect to its first taxation year ending after April 10, 1962 and the next succeeding four taxation years a corporation be permitted to deduct in computing income 150 per cent of the amount by which expenditures of a current and capital nature on scientific research in Canada incurred by it in the year exceed expenditures of a current and capital nature on scientific research in Canada incurred by it in its last taxation year ending on or before April 10, 1962.

That for the 1962 to 1966 taxation years both inclusive the deduction from tax allowed to corporations in respect of taxable income earned in a province be increased from 9 per cent to 10 per cent in a prescribed province in which arrangements exist for the replacement of federal grants to universities by additional provincial grants in accordance with the proposed amendments to the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act.

That with respect to taxation years commencing in 1962 a taxpayer be allowed a deduction from tax of an amount equal to the lesser of two-thirds of the amount payable for the year to a province as a tax on income from logging operations or § of 10 per cent of the taxpayer's income from logging operations in the province, and the right to deduct in computing income amounts paid to a province as tax on income from logging operations be repealed.

That with respect to expenses incurred after April 10, 1962 any corporation be allowed to deduct in computing income the drilling and exploration expenses, including all general geological and geophysical expenses, incurred by it on or in respect of exploring or drilling for petroleum or natural gas in Canada and the prospecting, exploration and development expenses incurred by it in searching for minerals in Canada not exceeding its income for the year from oil or gas wells in Canada.

That with respect to expenses incurred after April 10, 1962 an individual be allowed to deduct in computing income the drilling and exploration expenses, including all general geological and geophysical expenses, incurred by him on or in respect of exploring or drilling for petroleum or natural gas in Canada not exceeding his income for the year from oil or gas wells in Canada.
That with respect to acquisitions after April 10, 1962 amounts paid by

a corporation whose principal business is production, refining or marketing of petroleum, petroleum products or natural gas, or exploring or drilling for petroleum or natural gas, or mining or exploring for minerals,",,,,

at the end of my remarks, last night, that it was most urgently necessary that the twenty fifth parliament see to it, through its sovereign authority over its own institutions, that the Bank of Canada create credit and offer municipalities, which greatly need it, the means to borrow the necessary funds to carry out works essential in most of our communities.

When I am saying this, I am referring to the fact that in my own riding, for instance, most of the parishes which accepted the offer made last winter by the federal and provincial governments under the winter works program, had to float a heavy loan-in my own parish the loan was $90,000. The balance, after payment of borrowing costs, was $82,000, which was used to buy the materials required for the project. Once again, this year, an important part of the budgets of the municipalities will be earmarked for payment of interest on work carried out last winter, and for the next 25 years, the property owners in St. Joseph de Beauce will have to pay taxes or interest to financiers. Most of our municipalities now resort to winter works. But as they must purchase materials from companies, the federal and provincial governments collect over 11 per cent in manufacturing taxes, which is more than the amount of wages which the municipalities have to pay for carrying out municipal winter works.

It is also urgent, I think, that we take the necessary steps in order to promote the setting up of Canadian companies for the processing of our raw materials at home. Our country is rich with raw materials of all kinds. In the past few years a number of projects for the processing of our raw materials were submitted in the province of Quebec, such as a steel mill, for instance. We have all the labour force we need. There probably will be one million unemployed persons next winter.

Labour and material are available but these industries never become a reality in our province; they never go beyond the project stage. The province of Quebec, in co-operation with the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Dinsdale), could take steps to facilitate the provision of the funds required for the establishment of companies which would process our primary products instead of selling them as raw material to our southern neighbours, who after transforming them, sell them back to us at excessive prices, for we have to pay the added customs duty, taxes and import surcharges besides the cost of American labour.

For instance, I remember having learned in grade school that 75 per cent of the asbestos consumed throughout the world came from the province of Quebec, from the eastern townships area where Beauce county is located. If we consider that 75 per cent of the asbestos consumed and used in the whole world comes from our own province, would it not be time that Canadian companies obtained capital more easily in order to set up in our area industries which could manufacture, finish and process this raw material locally, instead of having trade imbalances which led to discussions of several days? Our trade relations with our neighbours to the south would not be adversely affected and we might have a favourable trade balance and thus enable the Canadian people to share in this wealth that belongs to them, the wealth of their own natural resources.

Mr. Chairman, I understand that several people are upset when there is a question of using the Bank of Canada to help obtain the credit required for processing our primary products in this country. Yet, we should not forget that tomorrow's economy will have to be a distributive economy, which will consist in distributing today's abundance without planning, because in this day and age new developments and science make production easy and fast.

We need a distributive economy which will take into account the purpose of industrial production in this country, as well as the necessity of processing our primary resources, as I said a moment ago, so as to put an end to our being controlled by international trade and foreign profiteers. In so doing, industry will be put back in its right place, in spite of what our socialist friends are thinking who state that the sole means to reach full employment in a country is planning.

We must give back to industry its true function, which is to produce the consumers' goods which the people need. Therefore, when speaking of a distributive economy, and of the Social Credit doctrine, which would help distribute abundance, I am thinking of the consumer, the ever-forgotten man in our Canadian economy, and it is on his behalf that we must work, through the distributive economy I just mentioned.

Mr. Chairman, if we study the information tabled in the house with regard to social legislation which now apply for the benefit of part of our population, I am of the opinion that the time has come to improve that legislation. It is true that in some circles nobody knows how to call the family allowances,
Income Tax Act

which were commonly called the ""baby bonus for the Quebec people"", but we must admit that they are a fundamental principle of distributive economy, which consists in recognizing to the fathers and mothers in this country the right to part of the wealth of their country, so as to enable them to have some bread on their plates.

Therefore, if the principle of helping large families to a better standard of living in this country of wealth and abundance is accepted one day, a comparison of living costs in 1945, when that legislation was passed, to those of today reveals that it is high time to double the rate of family allowances and to extend the age limit for the beneficiaries.

My fellow member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) suggested yesterday that we should help our young people get a better education by attending institutions of higher learning. Well, let us help educate those young people by letting them benefit from family allowances to a greater extent, by raising allowance rates while extending the age limit of beneficiaries to the whole schooling period.

2182654,ca.proc.d.1962-10-24.36.6,1962-10-24,279663fb-c05e-4f76-934e-36da39af24a9,ca.m.2855,Mr. Mather:,,INCOME TAX ACT,,,Mr. Chairman, the basis of our ways and means discussion seems to me to come down very simply to a consideration of how the government gets its revenue and what it does with it? To judge this we must have a perspective of the larger situation and consider the condition of the country which supplies and uses the revenue. In Canada today, Mr. Chairman, we suffer from division. This is the land of the great divide.

We are divided by great distances; we are divided physically by the great lakes, great prairies, great mountain ranges, two great languages, four great political parties and eleven great governments. Again we are divided further by our three levels of

administration, federal, provincial and municipal, and the basic rules for these last divisions were laid down so many years ago that they have less and less relation to the facts of life in 1962 and consequently condemn the taxpayers to friction, inefficiency, waste and frustration.

There are not many stories told about Canadians. We are not identifiable joke-wise as are the big Texans and the canny Scots, but I heard a joke the other day with reference to the matter under discussion here which I think more or less identifies the Canadian characteristic. There were an Englishman, an American, a Frenchman and a Canadian each of whom was asked to write an essay on the subject of the elephant. The Englishman wrote on the subject under the heading ""The elephant and the British Commonwealth;"" the American wrote under the heading ""Bigger and better elephants;"" the Frenchman wrote on ""The elephant and sex,"" and the Canadian wrote under the heading ""The elephant: Is it a provincial or federal responsibility.""

Mr. Chairman, it seems to me the time has come when we should give greater leadership towards ending this elephantine situation which divides Canadians at the three levels of administration, and we advocate immediate federal leadership towards realigning the confused administrative responsibilities at those levels.

Also, Mr. Chairman, we democrats point to another thing which divides us and renders all plans for a prosperous economy very difficult of attainment. This is the economic division of the country. We believe in democratic, economic planning for the welfare of all. We do not believe it is economic democracy when we have in Canada approximately 15 per cent of the population owning or controlling approximately 85 per cent of the wealth of the country, while 85 per cent of the population exists on approximately 15 per cent of the wealth.

A change is needed in this situation, a change towards planned, efficient development of our natural resources, and also a change is needed in the use which we make of our finance. Obviously what is physically possible in 1962 should also be financially possible.

We find in Canada today that 91 per cent of all Canadians, who are of age to do so, own no stocks at all. We find that 7 per cent of Canadians own less than $5,000 worth of stocks, and 2 per cent of the population own all the remaining stocks. Against this background let us examine the state of our revenues and expenditures so that we can understand the government's problems. Let us examine them as best we may, or as far as 27507-3-57
Income Tax Act
we can see them, because from what the Minister of Finance shows us in his periodic fiscal strip-tease it is very hard to see what they are.

As to the immediate nature of our ways and means, we find that in the largest economy move $85 million has been trimmed from defence spending as part of the effort to balance the books, an effort which has failed by something on the order of half a billion dollars. As my colleague from Na-naimo-Cowichan-The Islands said yesterday, this $85 million represents merely 5 per cent of what we are spending on defence. We are still pouring out over $1.5 billion on defence after the 5 per cent has been trimmed off, and according to the Toronto Globe and Mail we are not even saving $85 million, we are just $25 million below the actual defence spending of the previous period.

This is at a time when what the world needs is an example in peace and disarmament. It is at a time when more and more experts tell us there is no defence left in the nuclear world. This is at a time when we have staring us in the face an example of the futility of nuclear armaments to add one iota to the defence or security of an individual state or the world as a whole. It should now be obvious that nuclear armaments reduce security and add to the threat of international conflagration in direct line with the number of states which possess nuclear arms.

It is difficult enough for us to escape a nuclear international explosion if the states which possess nuclear arms are limited to three or four; but when 10, 20 or 30 states are given or secure nuclear arms then the likelihood of an explosion becomes more and more probable. I make these references to the futility of this country accepting or seeking nuclear arms, of course in line with our budget discussion, because the cost of such arms in dollars and cents will add stupendously to the load which our taxpayers will have to meet.

It should be interesting to the taxpayers of Canada to notice that at this time we are spending on so-called defence more than our combined federal expenditures on agriculture, fisheries, forestry, justice, labour, unemployment insurance, external affairs, the postal service and all public works at the federal level.

I say that since it has been possible for us to take a second look at defence expenditure and trim it by 5 per cent, then let us take a third look at the same item and trim it by a substantial worth-while amount. Then let us apply that saving to public benefit, either through the reduction of taxes at the middle
Income Tax Act

and lower levels of income, or through the payments of some of our debts, thus easing some of the crushing burden of interest, or through the establishment of a revolving credit fund by which the provinces and municipalities will be able to finance, at minimum rates, the carrying out of all those useful, publicly necessary projects which have been eliminated or postponed by the present misguided austerity program.

We of the New Democratic party hold both old line parties responsible for the sorry mess which we are in economically and financially, because it is the result not of five or ten years but comes near the close of 100 years of alternate Liberal-Conservative administration. Constructive expenditures on housing, schools, hospitals, and roads would bring back multiplied revenue to the treasury through the increased employment and increased industry which it would create. The treasury would benefit, it would not lose.

Specifically I advocate the imposition of a capital gains tax on stock market speculation profits. I have in my hand a leaflet put out by Argus Securities Limited of Vancouver, who are stock and bond people, which says:
Are you looking for tax free profits?
It goes on:

Canada is one of the few countries in the world where millions of dollars can be made in the stock market without paying a cent in capital gains taxes. Thousands of traders and speculators from all over have made fortunes in past years and will continue to do so because of our nation's unlimited wealth and natural resources. Find the easy way to get that extra cash, tax free. What you make you keep, all of it.

That document speaks for itself. I have no comment to make on it. I merely quote it to underline my contention that we are not acting intelligently or in the interests of Canada when we allow speculators to get off scot free with their gambling winnings in our stock markets. Let us have a capital gains tax on stock market speculations.

In regard to another aspect of our tax system, it is said that one reason why millions of Canadians have left our country for the United States is the extra inducement which that country holds out to them in the way of the realistic tax recognition it gives to the ordinary man's income and expenditures. It is a fact that in the United States the interest portion of all home mortgage payments, sometimes totalling hundreds of dollars a year, is deductible from income tax. The income on mortgage payments is reckoned separately and is filed by the income tax payer for deduction purposes.
The same thing applies to property purchases of any kind on the instalment plan. The United States treasury department
[Mr. Mather.l

exempts from taxation interest charges which are made on the instalment plan for the purchase of cars, radios, television sets, washers and furniture. The effect of this over the years has been, on the one hand to encourage the building or owning and furnishing of the family home, which is a vital unit in our way of life, and on the other to increase constructive industrial and commercial activity, and add to the employment of all kinds in many types of related business.

Mr. Chairman, I believe we would have a healthier country and a healthier treasury today if the following steps were taken. First, give leadership to this divided country toward realigning our maladjusted economic and administrative functions on the basis of 1962 rather than 1867. Second, take a hard, third look at defence spending and making a substantial saving in the hundreds of millions of dollars still being spent on that dubious item. Third, institute a capital gains tax on stock market speculative profits and exempt the interest portion of home and property instalment buying. Fourth, use all our energies to assist planning in the international as well as the internal sphere, whereby order will be brought out of the welter of trading and financial confusion that exists today.

In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, let me say that in my view there is a large section of thinking people in every political party in Canada today which favours Canada's making a very much enlarged contribution to the efforts of the United Nations and all its activities, toward the establishment of collective security.

Since September 15, purebred cattle breeders whose herds were certified against t.b. and checked free every year by federal veterinarians must keep their certification, have a private vet-
Income Tax Act

erinarian make tuberculine tests and pay tor his services. And the cost of keeping that certification is at the prorata of the number of heads in the herd of the breeder concerned. In the lower St. Lawrence region, nearly 150 breeders are affected.

And the minister also makes known a reduction of more than $1 million in government subsidies for the purchase of farm lime. Our soils are poor, our farmers want to enrich them to increase their production, and the government has no other answer than to reduce its assistance by $1 million. Also, the government has decided, through the Minister of Agriculture, that not a cent will be spent in the east of the country this year, for land drainage, irrigation works, etc.

In addition, the minister stated, a few days ago, that he would reduce support prices for dairy products if farmers did not cut their production voluntarily. In other words, he asks the farmers to kill their cows or to milk them once every two or three days. And he seems to think the thing possible. He threatens the farmers by announcing that if they do not cut their production voluntarily he will cut the support prices.

Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Agriculture is having a good laugh at eastern farmers. He announces with a great blowing of trumpets, that he will apply the ARDA plan, a legislation which has been discussed for the past four years, and on the other hand, without any previous announcement, he proceeds for instance, with all the cuts I just mentioned and a great many others which have not yet come out. The ARDA program will be paid for by the farmers themselves because the Minister of Agriculture said that, this year, he would spend $700,000 under that legislation, and the cuts in his budget will give him much more than that. One of my farmers told me during the week end, that he called the month of September, when the Minister of Agriculture made most of his decisions, ""black September"". I think he was right.

But the minister is always serene, always genial. He doesn't seem to realize the consequences of his action and that of his department. Do you know what the Minister of Agriculture reminds me of? He reminds me of that boxer who was saved by the bell; only, in his case, he was saved by the Chinese communists.

All those unfortunate, discouraging and depressing decisions were taken since the minister has appointed an assistant for eastern Canada, the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon). This means sacrificing a whole class of our society for a mess of pottage. And the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm seemed so smug, that he even declared in the house, in his speech on the address in reply:
It is the first time that a French Canadian holds such a post lor that department.
He meant that he was parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Agriculture. And, further on, on the same page, he said:
I shall thus have the opportunity ol being of greater service to the farmers of my country, to my fellow citizens in eastern Canada.

That is how, and I am recalling this for the benefit of my hon. friends opposite, the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Agriculture wants to improve the farming situation in eastern Canada, that is by cutting or curtailing all grants which might help the farmer class. AH the decisions I just mentioned, and many others which will be taken in the near future, or have been taken by the Minister of Agriculture and his parliamentary secretary, will have the result of discouraging the farmers. Therefore, I ask the members from the province of Quebec whether they are pleased today with their Minister of Agriculture, and I hope that if they did not have an opportunity of expressing themselves, they will do so before this discussion ends.
The hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Vincent), made the following statement in this house, on October 18, as found on page 664 of Hansard:
We, the Conservatives, are always practical people.
And he went on to say:

We know there is always room for improvement. .. improvements which we continually introduce because we can depend on the co-operation of a Minister of Agriculture who understands the needs of the eastern farmers-

Well, I wonder if he is still able to repeat the statement that he made right here in this house on October 18, in the light of the decisions taken by his minister, which will deeply affect agriculture in the province of Quebec, especially by discouraging a great number of farmers' sons who wanted to take over from their fathers. Such is not the case of the hon. member for Matapedia-Matane (Mr. Belzile) who gloated over the statements of the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Bechard). He attempted to prove that the soil of the Gaspe peninsula is not suitable for farming, when those people are working
steadily from morning till night to earn their living from that soil. Moreover, according to page 718 of Hansard, the member for Mata-pedia-Matane stated:
I would like to congratulate the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton) for his obvious dedication to the agricultural class.
But all these cuts in the budget, in all the items, will surely discourage the farmers.

And a little later, the hon. member stated that his Minister of Agriculture was kind-hearted. I can understand that he is kind-hearted, since he has taken him along to Rome for three weeks; however, I would rather see him display his kindheartedness for the farmers in the province of Quebec, many of whom will not be able to pass through the hardship that is now brought upon them.
And what do we find in the speech from the throne? We find the following:
The prosperity of agriculture remains essential to the well-being of the entire Canadian economy.

Mr. Chairman, those are fine words placed in the mouth of the representative of Her Majesty, but they are in direct contradiction with the facts and the unfortunate decisions of the Minister of Agriculture. And a little further, in the same speech from the throne, the government directs the representative of the Queen to say:

My ministers recognize that livestock is occupying a position of increasing importance in Canadian agriculture. They propose that a program be instituted to ensure the availability of storage facilities and continuity of supplies of feed grain to match the expanding requirements for livestock production, particularly in the areas of British Columbia and eastern Canada where supplies of feed grain are normally deficient.

Well, Mr. Chairman, at the very moment when those words were being spoken in the upper house, the Minister of Agriculture and his Quebec parliamentary secretary were cutting down the appropriations ordinarily provided for that purpose. This means, therefore, that the government will do less in that field, this year, than it has done in the past, while in the speech from the throne, it indicates it will do more.
Again, a little further, in the same speech from the throne, we note the following:
The program of rehabilitation and development of agricultural lands is proceeding actively and you will be asked to provide funds for it.
But we shall be called upon to vote reduced funds. So, how can you expect that the development of lands may be carried on more actively in 1962-63 than it has been in
Income Tax Act
previous years, when farmers will have less credit at their disposal?
A little further in the speech from the throne we note the following:
Legislation will be proposed to enlarge the funds of the Farm Credit Corporation, and allow greater flexibility in their use.
Mr. Chairman, that measure has been submitted to the house in the form of a resolution. Here is what is intended:

column1: premiums, subsidies and assistance measures. Now, since farmers won't be able to live otherwise than by contracting more debts, money will be lent to them at 5 per cent. And, with supreme irony, the Minister of Agriculture is announcing a national conference on agricultural apprenticeship, which is to be held this fall.
Mr. Chairman, how can our young people, those who have an agricultural vocation and who are about to inherit from their fathers, how can they have a rosy view of life?

What encouragement can they expect to get from this government which has made them pay for its extravagances, mistakes and lack of practical sense, in a situation calling for greater state assistance?

Mr. Chairman, I hope I have said enough to bring back the minister to better feelings, and convince him to review his policy. I would ask him to urge his leader to look elsewhere and not in the farmer's pockets for the money he will need to bring his deficit down to $540 million.

And if the minister cannot find, within his own party, a member fit to replace his parliamentary secretary from Quebec, because I suppose that, the present situation being what it is, the latter will have no choice but to abandon his post, if, I repeat, the minister is having some difficulty in finding among his friends a replacement for the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm, I hope he will not hesitate to take into consideration the sensible advice given him by members from this side of the house and especially by those who had the privilege of belonging to a government which, until 1957, gave agriculture a great deal of prosperity.

Before closing, Mr. Chairman, I must truly say that the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Agriculture should relinquish his post, if he does not wish to see his own electors asking him to do so.
I am not suggesting that he resign as member, for he is part of a government and I feel that a government should somehow reflect its members. He fits into the Con-

servative party and I believe he should remain there. But I do not think he is fit to be parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Agriculture, especially when one considers what the government intends to do to remedy an already sad situation which will be aggravated by the reduction of expenditures, those very estimates which were a source of hope for our farmers and on which they counted to balance their budgets.

Mr. Chairman, before I resume my seat, I ask once again that the Minister of Agriculture reconsider the situation, particularly the estimates of his department. I wonder if it would not be better if he asked the government to extend the austerity program by three or four days, so that he could not only recuperate the money that is to be taken away from him but also prevent the agricultural class from suffering more than it has during five years.

2182660,ca.proc.d.1962-10-24.36.12,1962-10-24,8eed4f27-aee9-4796-b78e-b81a57c98ee8,ca.m.7971,Mr. Ouellel:,,INCOME TAX ACT,,,We shall come to that, do not worry. We shall set it straight together.

Mr. Chairman, if we study the figures given to us on October 17 last when I asked what the debt of Canada was towards other countries and what amounts were due to us, we notice some quite frightening things. As a matter of fact, on December 31, 1960, the United States owed us $3.6 billion, the United Kingdom $1.5 billion and other countries, $1.9 billion. But that table is not quite so interesting when it indicates that in 1960, we owed the United States $18.1 billion, the United Kingdom $3.6 billion and other countries, $2.8 billion.

Mr. Chairman, I cannot quite understand that situation. If I am not mistaken, it was said that we had granted Great Britain a credit of about $7.5 billion. I cannot conceive how we made loans to that country at an interest rate of 2 per cent while we still owe the United Kingdom $3.6 billion. Yet, the matter of interest rates is one which should concern the administrators of this country.

It is absurd to get only 2 per cent interest from a country on a loan of $1 billion and be compelled today, because of the austerity program, to pay 6.2 per cent interest to the same country in a loan of $600 million made to us. As Canada's administrators, we shall claim exactly the same interest rates we are paying, that is, starting today, we shall ask these large countries to pay us the difference between 6.2 per cent we are paying and the 2 per cent we get from them.

Mr. Chairman, if Canada owes $26 billion to foreigners and if its assets outside the country total only $9 billion, we must admit that the situation is not very encouraging.

The figures show that the gross debt amounts to $22.9 billion. That is really something. Are we to blame the Conservatives and say that they accumulated that debt during the last five years? I do not think so. They will undoubtedly be able to take care of themselves, but they need not worry because I have a few words to say to them.

If we add to the national debt of $22 billion, the municipal debt which exceeds $4 billion, the provincial debt which exceeds $4.1 billion, the school board debt which amount to $4,175 billion, and the $722 million owed by private citizens either to banks or to finance companies, on October 19, 1962, the total is staggering. Furthermore, if we take into account the $1,698 billion, or nearly $1.7 billion, in the books of the Central Mortgage
and Housing Corporation, it is not surprising that we are living in a period that can be called a period of austerity, especially in view of the way we administer our finances.

One thing has been left out and I should like to hear some explanations in due course. Our central bank bears the name of Bank of Canada, but there is proof that it has never been at the service of Canada; it has worked only in the service of international finance, for foreigners and international transactions.
That is the principle opposed by Social Crediters because, even though we live in Canada today, we are not, in fact, master in our own country. Proof to bear out that statement is plentiful.

A former member of the Liberal party, who died last December, unfortunately, dissociated himself from his party during the war, because he felt that Canada was doing more than it could afford. However, we have today the evidence that we have done things for which we have to suffer the consequences. We did not win the war and we became friends with the Russians whom we shall have to fight some day. These are the results of our policy since 1939.
I believe that in 1939-and somebody will correct me if I am wrong-the debt was not much over $2 billion, when today we see debts piling up one on top of the other and always with foreigners.

I apologize for speaking In such a way, Mr. Chairman, but as Canadians we have served the interests of the imperialists instead of our own and today, they are simply transferred to our neighbours to the south, namely the Americans, who control about 85 per cent of our finances and industry.
We are not master in our country but we still have here everything we need to solve all our problems, and we must remember that we should have had some help from the Bank of Canada.

How can you explain that a loan is good for the Americans and other foreign countries, since it bears interest at 6 per cent, is not good for Canadians, under the same terms and simply with administration costs? We would certainly have the same results.
If we consider the total of our debts we notice that more than half of our income is used up just to pay interest to foreigners working against us.

I have here a report that I received at noon. It shows the unfortunate results of the last two wars, as it deals with 155,000 persons receiving a pension as a result of war injury. These people answered the call of their country and they have the right to live. However, in a country such as ours, I believe that we are overburdened with payments of all sorts.
In my opinion, if we pursue such a policy, whether we want it or not, a day will come, when the Canadian people will ask for a rendering of accounts.
That is exactly how certain democracies were lost, just because of irresponsible action on the part of their governments.

That is what the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fleming) accomplished by working in the interest of foreign countries when he held the finance portfolio in 1958. The Canadian people had painstakingly bought $6 billion worth of victory bonds bearing 3 per cent interest and becoming due a certain number of years later. What did the minister of finance do then? He converted those $6.5 billion worth of bonds and, according to newspaper reports, this operation cost Canada over $400 million.

However, the worse part of It is that the bonds that the people had to convert are now in the hands of financiers. The latter were given a reward of 3 to 4.5 per cent which cost Canadian taxpayers more than $90 million a year.
And yet, there are those who would have us believe that that was good administration. Well, let me tell you one thing. I, for one. think quite the opposite. I see things exactly as they happened.

The house is concerned with present events in Cuba. But what have we, Canadians, done? We have spent our time undertaking crusades abroad, very often in places where we had no business to be. And today, we are surprised at having to pay the consequences and at being in debt.
Those wars cost Canadian taxpayers over $50 billion. Why, I ask you?
Today, we are on the brink of bankruptcy, and what do we have to show for it?
I do not want to raise the racial issue because we are all Canadians whether we come from Newfoundland, Vancouver or the

province of Quebec. We want just one thing, and that is to live with all the other Canadians, no matter what their language or their race. We want to be Canadians first and before all, in the interest of Canada.

I live in the province of Quebec, and I cannot commend the federal government because we, French Canadians, have never been treated as we should have been. Now, there is some surprise to hear talk about separatism. Hon. members, if the French Canadians are not treated differently from now on and if the rights of the province of Quebec are ignored, separatism will become a reality one of these days.
I am not a separatist because, as Canadians, we have absolutely nothing to gain from separatism; but there is a limit to what people can stand. That is the situation at the present time.

I have here in my hand figures concerning my constituency and I see that during the last ten years more than 5,000 employees in the textile industry were laid off for the only reason that textile products are imported from foreign countries. Why is my region always the victim of the trade we make with other countries? I think that it should be another region's turn. Besides, it is clear that those foreign manufactures pay starvation wages and quite often their labour conditions are unreasonable.

The same conditions exist in agriculture. If industry does not pay high enough wages, the farmers in its neighbourhood cannot live either. At present, I think that the whole population in Canada-whatever is their mother tongue-think exactly the same way as I do, that the administration caters only to the big financiers of Canada or of foreign countries.
Today we are told that the doctrine put forward by Social Crediters, will bring about inflation. This makes me laugh.

I will describe a case which happened under the present administration, because we are not in office. About four months ago, the authorities of the city of Montreal called tenders from the Imperial Oil Company and others for 2 million gallons of gas to be used in its motor vehicles. What happened? This gas was sold at 12.89 cents a gallon while we pay 45 cents for it. If this transaction is examined in more detail, it will be discovered that after deducting income tax and municipal taxes this company can put money away for the future.

Therefore, it is imposition and taxes that cause inflation. What is the use imitating the ostrich and hiding our heads in the sand? The time has come for this government to change its policy. Let the government of Canada take back the power it gave to the Bank of Canada, let it lend money to Canadians without interest at cost only. Let the government lend funds, as many suggested before me, without charging interest, and only at cost, to cities, municipalities, school boards and provinces without infringing on their rights.
I am wondering whether we are going to keep on implementing the kind of economic policies we have at present.

Canadians should enjoy a tax reduction as my colleague stated. It would be easy with the income of the government to grant total exemption to all heads of family earning less than $5,000, and to all single taxpayers with incomes less than $3,000. It would be possible to grant increased old age pensions at age 65. Let us not forget that we have been generous with foreign countries, that we have in many instances welcomed as official guests honourable mendicants. We have been most generous to some foreigners, and, in my opinion, the Canadian people deserve an explanation from the government in this connection.

The Prime Minister's stand at the prime ministers' conference on the common market, which was held in England, was criticized. I am not competent to discuss such matters, but yet, one thing that surprised me is that the Prime Minister forgot that Canada has been independent since 1931, through the Westminster Statute, and that we were therefore entitled to make our own decisions. I actually admired the Prime Minister's response, but I blame him for not having had such thoughts before. Should he have thought that way we would probably not be in the situation we are now.

Now let us pass on to a matter I did not mention earlier. About the rights of minorities, anyone who comes to my town where there are French and English speaking people, all equally friendly to me and some of them my customers, people I see every day, is able to notice that those people know how to achieve national unity. If you want to learn the mechanics of national unity come to my riding and you will learn a wonderful lesson.

All these people were born in England, and oddly enough, we get along very well together. I believe that some people in this house are greater imperialists than the king himself. This often proved to be the case in the past. Some newsmen say that our system is topsy-turvy, but what ideas and policies have they upheld until now? They have defended a financial policy which is bad for Canada, and tried to have us believe that it was excellent.

At least, we have the courage to suggest something new. Give it a try, and if it does not work, then we shall see, but for Heaven's sake, give it a try, for we know that the old systems do not work. They are old, broken down horses.
Let me only quote a few words by Mr. Sales, the former president of the Ford Motor Company of Canada who said, two years ago, speaking before the Toronto board of trade:
Do away with politicians and economists and Canada will be a new country tomorrow.

And then, some people are surprised to see that some Canadians are unsatisfied. Frankly, 1 think some people do not catch on very quickly. A day will come when the people of Canada will claim their financial rights. Nobody ever claimed any such right before.

We are not blaming the members because, after all, they were elected by the people. We are gathered here, 265 strong, to watch over the nation and settle its financial problems. When you meet members of the other parties in the corridors, they will confess that they have no money, that they cannot even settle their own financial problems. Why should we side with their brand of politics and deceive 18 million Canadians? There is something wrong in your political system.

I have just received the economic policy of the present administration and that of the hon. members of the opposition who preceded them. Let us now turn to another point. The Prime Minister with all his responsibilities is paid $37,000 a year. Then, the presi-den of the C.N.R. gets $50,000 a year plus travelling expenses, and in the past five years he has been presenting us with deficits totalling $60 million. There was another man who received $50,000 a year, he was the president of the Bank of Canada. When he no longer was the right man, the hon. gentlemen opposite tried to dismiss him. So the 27507-3-58

Mr. Speaker, my explanation will be brief. The motion refers to Canadian families who in order to get an education, at the university or other level, and for some reason or other, have to live abroad. We all know that most of these people have reached a certain age, that they even have children. When they have to go to a foreign country to complete their education, they are deprived at once of the urgently needed family allowances.
I know of several cases, but I shall only tell you of one which is nevertheless quite
Family Allowances

typical. It concerns Canadian citizens of Dutch extraction who had to go to the United States in order to further their studies in their own language. While in the United States, the children lost their eligibility to family allowances, under section 4, paragraph 2(b), which provides that allowances are stopped as soon as a child is no longer a resident of Canada.

Therefore, in order to help the families of our young people who must go to school abroad for various reasons, either for a matter of language, as in this case, or simply for reasons of personal education, we thought that it might be advisable to put a special provision into the act so that those children could keep on getting family allowances even though they reside outside Canada.

I have no other explanation to give. I know that this matter comes under the purview of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith); maybe he has certain projects under way in that respect. In any case, I feel this motion should be considered in order to assist a number of our fellow citizens who must go abroad to complete their education.

If this resolution were passed, it would certainly be an aid to these people, so I will simply say that we support the idea. We also support the idea in the amendment. I should like to make one other comment at this time on private members' bills. I realize that it is the tradition around here that they all get talked out, at least invariably so. This seems to me too bad. 2182725,ca.proc.d.1962-10-24.37.1.53,1962-10-24,59589a84-9f74-4e1a-a40e-842ca444817c,ca.m.9652,Mr. Valade:,,FAMILY ALLOWANCES,TEMPORARY PERIOD OF ABSENCE OF CHILDREN FROM CANADA,,Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure for me to abide by the wise rulings you give concerning the younger members of the house and even concerning such a veteran as the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.

As I was saying at the beginning of my remarks, the resolution introduced by the hon. member of the opposition has some merit. Indeed, it causes us to wonder whether it would not be advisable to amend the Family Allowances Act.

Yet, it seems that the resolution is rather vague concerning the period of time a person would be allowed to spend outside of Canada for the purpose of education. I cannot conceive of a person studying abroad for one, two or even 10 to 15 years and then not returning to Canada even though his children have been getting family allowances all that time. Then the Canadian government would have paid non-resident children, enjoying the advantages of the foreign country, allowances coming from Canadian citizens' income.

I do not question the seriousness and the intentions of the hon. member who put forth this resolution which, I think, is more objective and sincere than the amendment which was introduced and, which was completely political in character and had no social importance whatsoever.

I cannot miss this opportunity to replace in its real context the statement made by the hon. member for St. James, who said that the Family Allowances Act was the result of the generosity of a former prime minister, the Bight Hon. Mr. King. To bear out his own statement, he quoted a former leader of the Conservative party and deplored his general attitude towards family allowances.

Mr. Speaker, I remember the time when the Conservatives opposed neither the act nor the principle of family allowances but rather the way the Liberals had planned it. Their attitude was an insult to the people of the province of Quebec. While we Conservatives asked for family allowances at climbing rates,
Family Allowances
the Liberals wanted decreasing rates. That was the issue that divided the Quebec members.
And such was Mr. King's policy.

We Conservatives tried to introduce more fairness into our legislation. Therefore the amendment to this resolution would certainly have been more serious if it had been presented as the hon. member suggested a moment ago, in the form of a bill rather than under the guise of a publicity trap. The introduction of a bill would have afforded the hon. member an opportunity of explaining why he wanted to amend the Family Allowances Act.
We are all in favour of family allowances.

I would even support family allowances adapted to economic cycles. Indeed, I am of the opinion that family allowances should be flexible and move with the cost of living, thus always ensuring a maximum allowance.
Family allowances render great services to families, and I think we are all anxious to find a formula that would take into account the variable requirements and economic conditions in our nation.

The resolution could have been more explicit as regards the duration of absence abroad for education purposes. It could have contained some provisions about the case of a person collecting allowances from our country for a certain period, then deciding not to return to Canada. This resolution could have incorporated some arrangements providing for a refund to the government of amounts paid for a number of years to persons who decide to remain outside of our country. In my opinion, we should be given an opportunity to consider this motion on another occasion when we might include certain provisions in line with what I have just suggested.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to repeat that if unemployment has increased in the city of Montreal and in the province of Quebec it is due to the sorry program put forward by the Liberals who were elected at the time of the provincial election.
